title: Jude and the Harvest
premise: Casper Marchetti has spent five years in the village of Harrow's End recording folk songs no one will sing twice, telling himself the night noises are pipes, wind, bad wiring. When the church bell—melted down in 1911—rings at midnight, the village's last resident, old Ada Voss, reveals the truth: in 1974 the village took a traveling family's land, their belongings, and their bell, and the family never left. As developers circle and Ada prepares to sign the sale papers, the dead grow louder, and Casper learns his own grandfather drove the truck that hauled the bell away. To survive, Casper must return what was taken—ringing the melted bell's twin at the family's unmarked graves before the papers are signed—accepting that justice outside the law will cost him the archive he came to make and the invisibility he hid behind. The novel ends with Casper staying in Harrow's End as its new bell-keeper, the village finally silent, and Ada's signature line left forever blank.
about_author: E. M. Montrose is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging oral histories in rural England, where more than one interview subject asked to have their words struck from the record. Jude and the Harvest is their second novel, written in a house they admit is probably haunted.

chapters.title: The Songs Nobody Sings Twice
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Establishes five years of fieldwork in Harrow's End: Casper records Ada Voss singing a harvest wassail, but she stops mid-verse, pale, and refuses to continue. That night Casper hears dragging footsteps in the empty lane. Emotional beat: quiet unease, the scholar's confidence beginning to crack.

chapters.title: Field Notes, Annotated
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Reviewing old recordings, Casper finds a second voice layered under Ada's—a child counting in a dialect the village no longer speaks. He convinces himself it's tape bleed. Emotional beat: rationalization as self-defense; the archive becomes both shield and trap.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. At midnight the church bell rings—one clear, wrong note. Casper checks the tower: no bell, no rope, only a scorched beam and a date scratched into the wall: 1911. Emotional beat: the moment explanation fails; wonder curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Ada's Ledger
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada reviews the village's hidden ledger of debts and sees the developers' contract waiting for her signature. She knows what the bell means and begins burning correspondence, deciding what truth can survive her. Emotional beat: weary guilt, a woman deciding how to end a story she helped begin.

chapters.title: What the Parish Register Omits
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. In county archives Casper finds the 1974 compulsory purchase order that seized the Aldery family's farm—and a photograph of the family, one child's face blurred as if the film refused him. Emotional beat: the thrill of discovery turning to complicity; he is cataloging a crime.

chapters.title: The Man Who Drove the Truck
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. A phone call home: Casper's mother mentions, offhand, that Grandpa Marchetti 'did a job up north in '74, hauling scrap.' Casper finds his grandfather's name in the bell's removal receipt. Emotional beat: inheritance as wound; the archive he trusted was built on his family's theft.

chapters.title: Jude
chapters.summary: Jude's POV (the Aldery child, in a voice of old, patient anger). We learn what happened in 1974: the family was driven out at harvest, the father died on the road, and the children stayed in ways the living don't. Emotional beat: grief given a body; the haunting reframed as a family waiting to be acknowledged.

chapters.title: The Village That Looks Away
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper confronts the remaining residents; they close ranks, insisting the Alderys 'sold up fair.' The pub goes silent when he enters. Someone leaves a dead blackbird on his doorstep. Emotional beat: isolation; the cost of asking questions in a village built on not answering them.

chapters.title: Ada Breaks the Silence
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada tells Casper the truth she's carried: she was the clerk who stamped the seizure, and the bell was melted to destroy the Alderys' claim-mark, the thing their land was 'answered by.' Emotional beat: confession as relief and terror; two keepers of the same secret finally facing each other.

chapters.title: The Papers Arrive
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. The developers' final offer lands; Ada, frightened by the bell's nightly ringing, is ready to sign and be done. Casper realizes the haunting will end either in erasure—the village sold, the graves paved—or in restitution. Emotional beat: the ticking clock begins; loyalty to Ada vs. loyalty to the dead.

chapters.title: What the Bell Was For
chapters.summary: Casper's POV, with Jude's voice intruding. Research in a folklorist's private papers reveals the bell wasn't decoration: it was rung at harvest to 'call the field's account,' a promise that the land's debts would be paid. Unpaid, it rings itself. Emotional beat: the folklore Casper studied was never dead; it was a contract.

chapters.title: The Twin
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper traces the bell's twin—cast from the same pour in 1911, sold to a decommissioned chapel two counties away. The chapel's caretaker warns him: 'That bell answers. Be sure of what you ask it.' Emotional beat: hope with a price tag; the possibility of return.

chapters.title: Night in the Chapel
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The Aldery dead gather at the chapel where their bell's twin hangs, waiting through the seasons as they have waited fifty years. Jude remembers his father's hands and the sound of the truck. Emotional beat: patience sharpening into need; the dead are not malicious, but they are done waiting gently.

chapters.title: The First Attempt
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper steals the twin bell at night, but the chapel bell is too heavy for his van, the road floods, and the village, tipped off, turns him back at the bridge. Ada, watching from her window, does nothing to help. Emotional beat: defeat; justice outside the law is harder than justice inside it.

chapters.title: Ada Signs—Almost
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. At the signing, Ada's pen hovers; the room fills with the smell of harvest and the sound of a bell that isn't there. She stalls, citing a missing survey. The developers give her one week. Emotional beat: courage at the edge of collapse; the last resident becomes the last obstacle.

chapters.title: The Village Turns
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. The residents, blaming Casper for stalling the sale, ransack his cottage and burn his recordings—except one reel survives in his coat. He realizes the village would rather be haunted than poor, and that he can't save both the archive and the Alderys. Emotional beat: loss of the old self; choosing truth over loyalty to the living.

chapters.title: The Grave Without a Stone
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Following the ledger's clues, Casper finds the Alderys' unmarked grave at the field's edge—four bodies, one small. He understands: the bell must be rung over them, the harvest account called, the debt named aloud. Emotional beat: grim clarity; the plan forms, and it will require witnesses.

chapters.title: The Long Road Back
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. With Ada driving and the reel of the Alderys' songs playing, Casper hauls the twin bell home through the night while the village's lights come on one by one behind them. Emotional beat: pilgrimage; two guilty inheritors doing the one thing the law never required and the dead always did.

chapters.title: Harvest Eve
chapters.summary: Climax. Multiple POVs converging. At the field's edge, Casper raises the bell as the villagers arrive to stop him—and as the developers' surveyor arrives to measure. He rings it once, names each Aldery aloud, and plays the reel of their songs. The ground answers; the melted bell's note sounds from the empty tower. Emotional beat: terrible, necessary release; the account is called.

chapters.title: What the Field Gave Back
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Dawn: no bodies, no ghosts—only the Aldery farm's foundations exposed, their names legible in the earth, undeniable to surveyor and villagers alike. The sale collapses; the land is registered to the Aldery estate. Emotional beat: exhausted awe; justice done outside the law, made undeniable inside it.

chapters.title: The Last Resident's Blank Line
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada tears up the contract, keeps the unsigned page framed on her wall, and teaches Casper the wassail verse she never finished. The village is quiet for the first time in fifty years. Emotional beat: peace earned, not given; the weight lifted from two generations.

chapters.title: The New Bell-Keeper
chapters.summary: Casper's POV, epilogue. A year later, Casper has become Harrow's End's bell-keeper, ringing the twin each harvest eve, recording a new archive: the songs the village finally sings twice. The last page of his field notebook reads simply, 'Paid in full.' Emotional beat: belonging after exile; inheritance transformed from debt into duty.
